turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for seeing me today, I really appreciate it. 

Um, well, I guess what brings me in is... well, it's a little embarrassing, and it's probably nothing major, but I've been having this issue where I just keep getting up when I'm really supposed to stay put. 

Like, I'm a private investigator, so I do a lot of sit-down client interviews, and I also do some tutoring, and... I just kind of pop out of my chair in the middle of them. Even at my book club! I always just thought of it as being energetic, or just needing to stretch my legs, you know? But... well, people are starting to notice. A few people have pointed out that I can't just sit and listen like everyone else does. 

I'd really hate for my clients or my friends to think I'm being rude or that I don't care about what they're saying. I just want to be a good listener for them. Does that make sense? Is that the sort of thing you might be able to help me with?

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they keep getting up and popping out of their chair during situations where they are expected to remain seated, such as client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in school, did you frequently struggle to stay in your seat during class when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... well, yes, I suppose I did. But I promise I wasn't a troublemaker or anything! I always tried really hard to be a good student. Um, if you look at my old grade-school report cards, they always said I was bright, which was so sweet of my teachers... but, well, they did usually have to add that I couldn't stay in my seat. Or wait my turn. 

My mother actually still jokes about it. She says I treated every single classroom like a crime scene that I just had to pace through and investigate. I always just chalked it up to being an eager, curious kid, you know? Not trying to be disruptive, just... very engaged. I hope that's the kind of background information you're looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right details.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient confirms they frequently struggled to stay in their seat during childhood, noting that report cards mentioned this and they would pace through classrooms.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly states that their childhood report cards noted they could not wait their turn.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the physical restlessness, do you find that you have trouble maintaining focus on tasks or conversations, often leading to you missing details or making careless mistakes?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I miss details. As an investigator, I'm actually very thorough! I have to be, right? I take a lot of pride in doing good work for my clients. 

I mean, sure, sometimes if a conversation goes on for a really, really long time, my mind might wander just a tiny bit, but I think that happens to everyone, doesn't it? I wouldn't call it making careless mistakes. I always double-check my reports and everything. I'm actually a very dedicated worker. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm bad at my job, because I really do try my best to be attentive. Does that answer your question okay?

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies missing details and making careless mistakes, stating they are very thorough and double-check their reports.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient denies significant difficulty sustaining attention, noting their mind only wanders a tiny bit during very long conversations, which they consider normal.

turns.doctor_question: In your daily life, do you find that you frequently interrupt others while they are speaking or blurt out answers before a question has been fully completed?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... well, I wouldn't say I *interrupt*, exactly. I just... I get very enthusiastic, I suppose? 

Like, if I'm at the office and I hear some of the junior detectives discussing a lead, or even if I'm just out and hear a neighbor talking in the hallway, I tend to just... jump right in. I'll offer some advice or ask a few questions to try and help them out. I just want to be helpful, you know? 

But... well, sometimes after the fact, I do realize that maybe I wasn't actually asked to join in. I guess I kind of barge into their conversations without meaning to. I always feel terrible afterward, because I really don't want to be overbearing or rude. I just get so caught up in trying to be a good neighbor or a supportive colleague. Is that the sort of thing you mean? I hope that doesn't make me sound too nosy!

symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to frequently jumping into and barging into others' conversations uninvited, which is a clear manifestation of intruding on others.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find that you lose or misplace items necessary for your tasks, such as your keys, wallet, or important work documents?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... no, I wouldn't say I *lose* things. I'm actually very organized! I have a whole system for my files and everything. 

I mean, I suppose everyone misplaces their keys now and then, right? Sometimes I might set my notebook down on a different desk while I'm talking to someone, and it takes me a minute to remember where I left it. But I always find it! It's never really a big problem, and I certainly don't lose important evidence or anything like that. I'm very careful about my work materials. 

I hope that makes sense? I just don't want you to think I'm careless or irresponsible, because I really do take my job very seriously. Am I giving you the right kind of examples?

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly states they do not want the doctor to think they are careless and that they take their job very seriously.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient states they are very organized and have a whole system for their files.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies losing things, stating they always find misplaced items and never lose important work materials.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel the need to get up and move, do you feel an internal sense of restlessness or a physical 'itch' that forces you to move, or is it more of a reaction to your environment?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... I wouldn't really call it an "itch." That sounds so... uncomfortable, doesn't it? I think it's more just that I have a lot of energy and a really strong work ethic! I just like to be productive. 

Like, even on days when I don't have active field work, I'm still always doing *something*. I'll go straight from unpacking boxes at the office to completely reorganizing my old case files, and then I'll be right out the door running errands. My friends joke that I tackle my downtime like I'm chasing a hot lead! 

I just... well, I suppose I do have a little bit of a hard time just being "off duty" and relaxing on the couch. I always feel like there's something useful I could be doing instead. But I think that's a good trait for an investigator to have, right? It means I'm always on top of things! Does that answer your question okay? I just don't want you to think I'm bouncing off the walls or out of control, I really just like to stay busy!

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes being constantly on the go, having a lot of energy, moving from one task to another without stopping, and having a hard time relaxing or being 'off duty', which aligns with acting as if driven by a motor.

turns.doctor_question: When you jump into conversations or move around in meetings, do you often find that you do these things even when you have explicitly promised yourself or others that you will stay quiet or stay in your seat?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... well, no, I wouldn't say I break promises like that. That sounds a bit... defiant, doesn't it? I really try to be respectful of everyone's time and space. 

If someone specifically asks me to hold my questions until the end of a briefing, or if I know a meeting is meant to be very formal, I definitely do my best to follow the rules. I might shift in my chair a bit, or maybe jot down a lot of notes so I don't forget what I wanted to ask, but I don't just ignore what I've promised to do. 

I mean, I suppose there might have been a time or two where I got a little too excited about a breakthrough in a case and spoke up a second before I was supposed to, but... it's never because I'm deliberately trying to be disruptive! I always try to be a good team player. Is that the kind of thing you're asking about? I really hope I'm not coming across as someone who doesn't listen to instructions!

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient admits that they might shift in their chair during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly denies ignoring rules or failing to follow instructions when asked to behave a certain way.
